title: The environment
hookLine: plant a tree, and whatever eats from it counts as charity for you
tomorrow: what did a thirsty dog teach a man at a well?

cards: Saturday, seven in the morning, a sign-up sheet for a tree planting. The saplings are knee-high. The shade they'll make is years away, long after the volunteers have moved on.
So why bother? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ answered with a strange kind of accounting. Don't count the shade.

teach.h: A BIRD, A PERSON, AN ANIMAL.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari: no Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, but it counts as sadaqah, charity, for him. Every bite. The sparrow pecking a fig.
One version in Sahih Muslim even adds: what's stolen from it counts too. So the tree is worth planting even if you never sit under it. The reward was never the shade.
It's what the tree gives away.

teach.h: PLANT IT, EVEN AT THE HOUR.
teach.b: A saying in al-Adab al-Mufrad pushes it to the edge: if the Hour comes and one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it.
The Qur'an puts people in charge of the earth, not as owners. In Pickthall's words: "He it is Who hath placed you as viceroys of the earth." A viceroy looks after what belongs to someone else.
Now look back at the week. It has the tree's shape: a plate, a stopped hand, a true word, a steady hour, a Sunday call, an open door. Each one feeds someone you may never see again.

how: Muslims plant trees, keep gardens and give fruit away with this hadith in mind, and some mosques and Muslim groups organize tree plantings and clean-ups as acts of sadaqah.

o: the living world given into our care
wild land that belongs to nobody at all
the weather and the seasons God sends

games.q: the week's lines — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith counts it as charity only when people eat from your tree
a bird, a person or an animal: every bite counts.
one saying says to plant your sapling even if the Hour has come
that's the report in al-Adab al-Mufrad.
caring for the earth is a modern idea with no roots in the hadith
the Prophet counted every bite from a planted tree as charity.

games.q: your neighbor's peach tree hangs over the sidewalk, and kids grab peaches on the way to school. she's annoyed and wants the branch cut back. what does today's hadith offer her?
o: every peach those kids eat counts as charity for her, the hadith says.
the kids are taking what isn't theirs, so cutting it back is the answer.
it only counts as charity if she hands the fruit out on purpose.
games.why: a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, and it's charity for the planter. one version in Sahih Muslim adds: even what's stolen from it.

practice: Count, slowly, the living things that fed you today without knowing it: the wheat in the bread, the tree behind the paper, the bee somewhere behind the honey. Give each one a breath, as many as come.

wordCard.voice: The environment: the living world in our care. In the hadith, whatever eats from what you plant counts as charity.

orig.note: Arabic: charity, any good given freely; the hadith's word for every bite.

carryVoice: Something to keep: every bite is charity, even the ones you never see. That's the week, planted.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2320 (also Sahih Muslim 1553): no Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, but it is charity for him
Sahih Muslim 1552 (the version adding: what is stolen from it is charity for him)
al-Adab al-Mufrad 479: if the Hour comes and one of you has a sapling in his hand, let him plant it

sources.q: He it is Who hath placed you as viceroys of the earth
